prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping, which opened a new regime of precision in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a clean idea (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift and puts atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime) with a demanding, independently reproduced realisation at the 10^-18 level, driven decisively by Ye's group through systematic-error control and the study of collective and many-body shifts. The impact is concrete and measurable: the roadmap to a redefinition of the SI second, relativistic geodesy, and sharper tests of fundamental constants and of physics beyond the Standard Model. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, a natural two-person prize with no forced cut among credited names, whereas B027, B038 and B015 each force a contestable selection. The field is mature enough that no one doubts the result, and it is not yet recognised in any adjacent prize in its own right.
statement.case_against: The 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (control of single ions, which also enabled the best ion clocks) cover neighbouring ground, so it must be argued that lattice clocks are a distinct achievement and not a refinement of recognised work. Other groups (ion clocks, Lemonde, Lisdat, the JILA Kimble/Ludlow line) also have claims that a two-name credit leaves out. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and this ballot has the narrowest base of support: only four members ranked it, and one placed it eighth. Meanwhile B050 is ranked by six members, four in the top three, so my first place may simply reflect my own specialty.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: original and conceptually clear, at the 10^-18 level, with Katori and Ye as a natural pair, though the redefinition of the second is pending and the 2005 comb prize is adjacent.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and on the pairing, and your caveat about the pending redefinition is the right one. I would resist treating it as a reason to wait: the clocks are reproduced in many laboratories with routine international comparisons, so the physics no longer depends on the SI decision. Where I would go further than your opening is the 2005 overlap. The comb prize rewarded the ruler; lattice clocks rewarded a new way of making the oscillator itself, with a many-body-limited error budget. The committee should state that distinction in the citation, not assume it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the lattice clock only eighth, noting that the 2005 and 2012 prizes in related precision measurement may affect its priority, and that Ludlow and Kimble contributions are not credited. Her first place is the quantum cascade laser.
responses.response: The priority concern is fair and is the strongest argument against my first place. I think it is answered by what was actually invented. The magic-wavelength condition is a new principle that made neutral-atom ensembles competitive with single ions, which the 2012 prize did not do. On Ludlow and Kimble, I accept that the credit is not exhaustive, but that is true of nearly every candidate here, including your B021 (Kazarinov and Suris). I do not think it distinguishes B051 from the others.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B050) first as a clean and original discovery with two decades of independent confirmation, while acknowledging that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are left out and that 2016 honoured topological phase transitions.
responses.response: I take B050 seriously: it is my own alternative, and its breadth of support, six members of eight, is greater than anything I can claim for B051. My reservation is attribution. The Molenkamp experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp prize leaves out the people who told the experimentalists where to look. You call this unallocated credit, but I think it is a defect in the prize itself, not a footnote. Even so, I accept that it is a closer call than the clocks, and I would not oppose B050 if the committee can settle the credit.

responses.point: Pearce ranks lattice clocks fifth, calling the two-name configuration natural and the timing good, but notes that Ye also appears on other candidates and might overlap with other recognition.
responses.response: Ye's appearance elsewhere does not weaken this ballot; the credited achievement here, the lattice clock with its stability and collective-shift control, is his own, and I would credit it on those grounds alone. I would however accept your point that the committee should avoid confusing the question of overlap with comb-related recognition by keeping the citation specific to the lattice clock. If the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition, I would want that decision made explicitly and not by default.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, with strong confirmation and architecture used across superconducting processors, while noting that it sits close to the 2025 circuit prize and that Girvin and Blais are not separable.
responses.response: I agree that cQED is original and has had large impact, but the proximity to the 2025 prize and the forced choice among four names make it hard to defend this year. I would also separate the foundation from the application: the larger case for superconducting quantum computing is still developing, so the committee would be honouring an architecture whose payoff is not yet settled.

uncertainties: Whether lattice clocks are judged a distinct achievement from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or a refinement of them.
Whether the committee should wait for the formal redefinition of the second before awarding.
Whether B050 should displace B051 given its much broader opening support, and whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission can be resolved.
Whether credit for the lattice clock should extend beyond Katori and Ye, for example to other lattice-clock groups.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for Katori or Ye. My documented collaborations (Lund and ETH attosecond groups, L'Huillier, Keller, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) do not include either candidate. I am a theoretical atomic physicist, so my field proximity to precision atomic spectroscopy is a source of bias, not a formal conflict.
